Title: A Timeout Is Not a Failed Action: Chaos Testing AI Agent Tool Calls
Abstract: Chaos engineering is most valuable when it tests assumptions that ordinary success-path metrics cannot reveal. This session injects a deterministic lost response after an AI agent's mutating tool has committed an external effect. The agent observes a timeout, retries with a fresh request ID, and produces two effects for one logical operation. Using a public MCP reproduction and independent third-party replication, the session distinguishes transport request identity, logical-operation identity, and durable effect state. It compares caller-supplied idempotency keys, server-local ledgers, downstream cooperation, and reconciliation through independent read-back. Each defense has limitations: reserving a key does not establish that an external effect completed, and missing read-back does not necessarily establish non-execution. Attendees leave with a fault-injection matrix, positive and negative controls, and a recovery decision tree for safe retry, reconciliation, and explicitly unknown outcomes.

Title: Chaos Engineering for AI Agents: Breaking Permissions, Tools, and Context on Purpose
Abstract: Agent systems fail in ways traditional chaos experiments don’t cover. A user loses access mid-session, but the agent still holds their data in context. A tool times out, and the agent quietly switches to a different path that returns more than it should. Teams discover these behaviors in production because nobody tested for them.  This talk applies chaos engineering principles to multi-agent systems, drawing on experience building agents with custom MCP servers over enterprise banking CRM data. It covers:  Revoking entitlements mid-session to test whether cached context is revalidated Injecting tool failures and latency to observe how agents reroute and what data the fallback paths expose Returning partial or denied results to check whether the agent leaks information through its reasoning Defining steady state for agents, including what “safe behavior” means beyond uptime Running experiments safely with synthetic users and generalized data  Attendees will leave with a starter set of agent chaos experiments and the hypotheses behind each one.

Title: When Agents Fail in Production: Incident Stories and Recovery Patterns
Abstract: The most instructive production lessons come from things breaking. This talk is a field guide to agentic AI incidents drawn from running multi-agent systems in production at retail scale: the agent that confidently presented hallucinated inventory numbers to merchants, the runaway tool-call loop that burned a week's inference budget in an afternoon, the silent data drift that corrupted outputs for days before anyone noticed, and the cascading failure when one agent's bad output poisoned every downstream step. For each incident: what broke, how it was detected (or why it wasn't), the recovery playbook, and the engineering change that prevents recurrence. Attendees leave with a catalog of failure modes to defend against and detection patterns that catch them early.

Title: Chaos for Coding Agents: Deliberate Failure Modes Before They Hit Production Review
Abstract: Agents fail differently than services — silent wrongness, tool misuse, and cascading “helpful” changes. This talk adapts chaos thinking to agent workflows: inject bad tool results, revoke permissions mid-task, force prompt/skill regressions, and measure blast radius in review time and escape defects. How staff engineers design safe experiments so teams learn agent limits before customers do. For engineers who ship agents, not academic chaos tooling demos.

Title: Your AI Agent Passed Every Eval. What Happens When a Tool Call Times Out?
Abstract: [Disclaimer: The opinions, insights, and perspectives shared in this session are solely my own and do not reflect those of my current or past employers, nor do they convey any confidential information by any means.]  Overview: Chaos engineering taught us not to trust the happy path for services. Agents need the same discipline. When an agent's tool call times out, the write may already have committed, and a retry may become a duplicate charge. When a read-back is stale, the agent may "repair" something that was never broken. When a call returns ok after half the work, the agent reports done. None of this shows up in an eval where every tool answers cleanly, and every one of these faults is routine in production.  Structure: Part 1: The steady state is the real state, not the agent's report. Chaos experiments start from a steady-state hypothesis. For an agent, that hypothesis has to be written against the backend (exactly one charge, fulfillment applied), and the agent's own claim gets scored separately. Two numbers, not one: what landed, and what the agent said landed.  Part 2: A fault taxonomy for tool calls. Timeout after commit, delayed visibility, partial success, and stale conflicts, injected at low, medium, and high rates taken from published failure measurements (Mansoor et al.). Where to inject them: in the tool, in a proxy between the agent and an MCP server, or in the backend. How to keep the blast radius small: seeded faults, sandboxed state, and containers for any third-party tool.  Part 3: Metrics that a clean run hides. Duplicate-action rate, silent-failure rate (reported success, wrong state), an explicit "unconfirmed" rate, and pass^k, the chance a task succeeds k times in a row. In agent-fault-lab (MIT), 3,200 seeded episodes per row: an idempotency key alone still left 9.9% silent failures; a read-back alone was fooled by delayed visibility; only a key plus a polled postcondition check plus an "unconfirmed" outcome held at 0.0% silent failures and 98.5% pass^8. These are scripted policies, labelled as such, and the harness is how you measure your own agent.  Part 4: Demo and game day. A live run: inject a lost response, watch a retry agent report success while the ledger shows two charges, then rerun the same seed against the verified design. We close with a one-page game-day plan for an agent team.  Attendees leave with: 1. Steady State Against Real State: score what landed and what the agent claimed as two separate numbers 2. The Tool-Call Fault Taxonomy: four faults, three intensities, and where to inject each one 3. pass^k Over pass@1: one clean run proves almost nothing about an agent you'll run thousands of times 4. The Unconfirmed Outcome: give the agent a sanctioned "I can't confirm it" instead of a confident guess 5. A Harness to Run Today: agent-fault-lab, standard library only, no API keys  A green eval only tells you the agent works when nothing fails. Production is where things fail.  Sources: 1. agent-fault-lab (results table and method): https://github.com/MuhammadMoeezKhan/agent-fault-lab 2. Mansoor, Phadke, Rana, "Verified Tool Calls Improve LLM Agent Reliability Under Non-Atomic Failures," arXiv:2608.02645, 2026 (fault types and rates). 3. tau-bench, the pass^k estimator (Yao et al., 2024).

Title: Breaking the Brain: Chaos Engineering for AI-Native Apps on AWS with Datadog
Abstract: Abstract  AI-native applications fail differently from traditional services. A Bedrock throttle, a slow tool call, a stale vector index or an agent stuck in a retry loop rarely produces a clean 500. More often you get a confident wrong answer, a quietly tripled token bill or a workflow that never finishes. Classic chaos experiments (kill an instance, add latency) are necessary but no longer sufficient.  This presentation focus how to run chaos engineering on AI-native workloads hosted on AWS and observed with Datadog. We start with a failure-mode taxonomy for LLM apps and agents:  model throttling and regional unavailability latency and timeout cascades tool and MCP failures RAG and vector-store degradation context or prompt poisoning runaway token and cost loops  Then we turn each one into a testable hypothesis. You’ll see how to inject faults using AWS Fault Injection Service plus an application-level fault layer. You’ll also see how to use Datadog LLM Observability, APM traces, monitors and SLOs to confirm the system degrades the way you expected. We finish with a demo of an agentic application on AWS taking a controlled failure, and how guardrails, fallbacks and circuit breakers held up (or didn’t).  You’ll leave with a repeatable experiment template and a starter set of Datadog signals for the resilience of any AI-native system.  Key takeaways  - A failure-mode catalogue for LLM apps and agents, beyond “the API returned an error” - How to define steady state and hypotheses for non-deterministic systems, using quality, cost and latency SLOs - A practical approach combining AWS FIS and app-level fault injection to test models, tools and retrieval - Which Datadog signals confirm a failure was contained: traces, LLM spans, token and cost metrics, and monitors tied to SLOs - How to run game days for AI teams safely, with blast-radius limits and rollback

Title: Your System Is Resilient. Is Your Organization?
Abstract: The most dangerous failures are often the ones that have not fully failed yet.  Latency rises. Retries multiply. Capacity starts to tighten. Nothing is fully down, and the signals are still ambiguous.  Now the harder question appears: who decides that the system is heading in the wrong direction—and who has the authority to act before failure becomes obvious?  This session explores resilience at that boundary between technical degradation and organizational response. We’ll look at how teams recognize early failure signals, make decisions with incomplete information, and avoid the hesitation that turns a recoverable condition into a major incident.  Chaos engineering is designed to expose assumptions before production does.  One of the most important assumptions to test is whether the organization can act while there is still time.

Title: Organizational Chaos Engineering: Stress-Testing Financial & Operational Systems in Tech Companies
Abstract: Chaos engineering teaches us to intentionally inject failure into distributed systems to uncover hidden weaknesses before they cause catastrophic outages. But why do we limit this discipline to servers and microservices when tech businesses frequently fail due to operational, financial, and unit-economic breakdowns?   I apply the principles of chaos engineering and resilience testing to tech business operations and capital management. Drawing from real-world experience scaling deeptech and hardware-software enterprises, this talk demonstrates how to stress-test your business model, identify single points of failure in unit economics, and build an operationally resilient organization capable of surviving market shocks and sudden cash burn spikes. The structure of the talk: - How to apply SRE and chaos principles to financial modeling, unit economics, and operational workflows.   - Identifying "single points of failure" in team capacity, project budgeting, and plan-vs-actual execution.   - Frameworks for managing burn rate during fundraising rounds and avoiding hidden systemic risks.   - Establishing clear operational metrics that tell you when to pivot, restructure, or safely terminate unprofitable initiatives.

Title: You Build It, You Run It Is Dead: Reliability When the Author Is an Agent
Abstract: You build it, you run it. Fifteen years of SRE gospel, and almost nobody questions it.  The rule was never about writing code. It was about a loop. Whoever wrote it understands it, so whoever wrote it carries the pager. Understanding was the point. The pager was just enforcement.  Agents cut that loop. The code still ships. The author is gone.  I take the assumption apart, one joint at a time. No human author, so who holds the pager. Nobody who can explain it, so the author cannot answer the 3am question. Review cannot keep up with the output, so your gate is a rubber stamp.  Then the fixes that do not work, and why each one folds. Human in the loop. Make the agent better. Keep agent code out of prod.  Then the reframe. If writing it no longer means understanding it, reliability has to come from somewhere else. Operability stops being something you hope the author cared about, and becomes something you check for.  One real incident carries the argument. A single S3 copy call, a 5 GiB limit nobody checked, a migration that never sealed, and a cluster crash-looping while the log line said `migrating objects: <nil>`. None of it was hard. Nobody could see it.  The principle is not dead. The assumption under it is.

Title: Your Monitors Approved Every Bad Fix: What Happened When AI Agents Repaired 64 Broken Pipelines
Abstract: AI agents are starting to fix production incidents, so we tested one on purpose. I built PipeMend, an open benchmark of 64 broken data pipelines, and let Claude agents of three sizes diagnose and repair them.  The uncomfortable result: production-style monitors approved every harmful fix the agents made. Row counts looked fine, jobs went green, and the data was wrong. The best warning sign wasn’t the monitoring at all. It was the agent’s own confidence score.  This talk walks through the experiment like a chaos game day: how the failures were injected, where the agents fixed the symptom instead of the cause, and why “the job succeeded” is the wrong check for AI-made changes. I’ll close with pipeverify, an open-source tool and GitHub Action that checks a pipeline change against the source data before it ships.  You’ll leave with a practical rule for letting agents touch production: decide whether to fix or page based on evidence, not green dashboards.

Title: Engineering Resilient Data Pipelines for Commissions and Trade Intelligence
Abstract: In financial data systems, pipeline failures, data inconsistencies, and processing delays can directly affect commission payouts, trade reporting, and regulatory compliance. Building resilient data architectures is essential to maintaining accuracy, reliability, and operational continuity.  This session explores practical approaches to engineering fault-tolerant data pipelines for complex commissions and trade environments. Attendees will learn how modern ELT architectures using platforms like Snowflake organize raw, refined, and curated data layers to support reliable processing, reconciliation, and near real-time reporting.  The discussion examines common engineering challenges, including high-volume trade processing, complex commission hierarchies, missing or inconsistent records, and failures in data transformation workflows. It highlights validation frameworks, exception handling, reconciliation processes, and data lineage tracking as essential techniques for detecting issues, limiting their impact, and maintaining data integrity.  The session also covers modernizing legacy ETL systems such as DataStage while preserving critical financial business logic. Emphasis is placed on observability, scalable architecture, governance, and collaboration across engineering, finance, and compliance teams.  Attendees will gain practical insights into designing reliable, auditable, and maintainable data pipelines that reduce operational risks and support accurate financial reporting.

Title: When API Tests Aren’t Enough: End-to-End Testing a Live Dota 2 Data Pipeline
Abstract: In the high-stakes world of live esports broadcasting, showing incorrect draft data in a live widget isn't just a bug — it's a ruined viewer experience. To deliver real-time Dota 2 pick/ban data, we built a complex pipeline relying on Game State Integration (GSI). This system takes state snapshots, restores sequence events, maps internal entities, and pushes updates via WebSockets to a frontend widget.  We quickly realized that traditional unit and integration tests were insufficient. We could validate parsing, mappings, and WebSocket contracts, but a correct HTTP payload didn't mean a correct widget. A hero identifier could be mapped perfectly in code, but still display the wrong asset on the screen.  In this talk, I will share how we bridged the gap between protocol correctness and product correctness. Instead of relying on artificial JSON fixtures, we turned the actual Dota 2 client and known game replays into our primary E2E test fixture. You'll learn how to test an entire delivery chain — from raw game data to network transport and frontend rendering — in a single loop, and how we empower operators with a "Test to Live" config check to prevent production disasters caused by unexpected game mode semantics.  Ultimately: if the user sees the widget, the widget is what you should test.

Title: Zero-Latency UX with JSON Mirrors: Rethinking Data Access Beyond the Backend
Abstract: Modern web applications often accept a fundamental assumption: every meaningful user interaction requires a round trip to the backend. This talk challenges that assumption through a concrete, production-grade case study, building nana.events, a blazing-fast event discovery platform powered by a PHP server and a relational database.  Despite relying on a traditional stack, the system achieves near zero-latency user experience by restructuring how data is delivered and consumed. Instead of treating the backend as the primary query engine at runtime, the server continuously produces two static JSON artifacts: a comprehensive dataset and a smaller, lightweight subset. These files act as precomputed, optimized views over relational data.  At runtime, the browser becomes the execution engine. All filtering, searching, and navigation occur client-side, eliminating repeated network calls and dramatically reducing latency. The large JSON file enables full functionality under normal conditions, while the smaller file serves as a resilient fallback under constrained or unstable network conditions.  This session walks through the architectural decisions behind this approach, including data shaping strategies, trade-offs between freshness and performance, memory considerations in the browser, and techniques for maintaining consistency between relational and static representations. We will also discuss when this model breaks down and how to measure its effectiveness.  Rather than introducing new infrastructure or exotic technologies, this talk demonstrates how rethinking data flow, shifting computation to the edge, and precomputing aggressively can unlock significant performance gains even in conventional environments.

Title: Why Database Migrations Fail Silently
Abstract:
A database migration can look successful on launch day and still leave
behind problems that surface weeks later. The new database is running,
traffic has moved, and the dashboards look healthy. Yet some records
may already be inconsistent.

Having worked on large-scale database migrations, I've seen how
difficult it can be to catch these problems before they affect
customers.

In this talk, I'll cover five failure modes that are easy to miss
during zero-downtime migrations, including dual-write inconsistencies,
backfill races, schema drift, delayed events, and incomplete
validation. I'll explain why common checks fail to catch them and how
teams can use fault injection, record-level reconciliation, shadow
reads, and controlled rollouts to uncover problems earlier.

The goal is to give engineers practical ways to test migration safety,
detect silent failures, and know when it's safe to cut over.

Title: Breaking Things Safely at Scale: Configuration Canaries and Dependency Isolation at Meta
Abstract: At large scale, most outages don't come from code. They come from configuration changes that take effect everywhere in seconds, and from shared dependencies whose failure spreads to everything built on top of them. At Meta, I worked on both problems for revenue-critical advertising infrastructure that handles thousands of changes a day and millions of requests per second.   This talk covers two practices that came out of that work. First, configuration canaries that judge a change by business signals, such as whether ad events are still being recorded correctly, and not only by system health, because a change can pass every CPU and error-rate check while quietly breaking the data a business depends on. Second, dependency isolation for shared services: isolating the parts of each record that depend on a shared tier, giving critical traffic its own limits, and recovering failed work afterward, so one shared-service failure doesn't cascade.   Attendees will leave with practical patterns they can apply to their own rollout and dependency design.

Title: When a Region Fails: Chaos Engineering for Multi-Region Kafka
Abstract: Designing a distributed system to survive failures is one thing. Proving that it can continue operating when an entire region becomes unavailable is another.  This talk explores the architecture and failure-testing strategies behind highly available, multi-region Apache Kafka deployments supporting mission-critical workloads. We'll examine how broker placement, replication factors, in-sync replica requirements, and KRaft controller quorums influence availability and durability during regional outages.  Using concrete architectural examples, we'll walk through failure scenarios including regional isolation, broker loss, controller failures, and network degradation. We'll also explore how to validate recovery behavior, maintain write availability without compromising durability, and identify failure modes that traditional monitoring may miss.  Attendees will leave with practical techniques for designing resilience experiments, evaluating failure-domain independence, and building confidence in distributed messaging systems before real incidents occur.  Key takeaways: - How to design multi-region Kafka replication and controller quorums for regional fault tolerance. - How to conduct controlled failure experiments involving brokers, network partitions, and regional outages. - How Kafka's ISR, acknowledgments, and quorum configurations influence durability and availability. - How to validate recovery, not merely detect failures. - Practical lessons for turning architectural resilience assumptions into testable guarantees.

Title: Engineering Race-Condition Resilience in Distributed Systems
Abstract: Race conditions are a critical reliability challenge in distributed systems, where concurrent transactions, delayed events, and unpredictable execution sequences can produce inconsistent data, duplicate updates, lost transactions, and operational failures. These problems become particularly difficult to diagnose and recover from in cloud-native, event-driven architectures.  This session presents a practical architectural framework for reducing race conditions and improving system resilience under concurrent workloads and failure scenarios. The approach combines five capabilities: deterministic sequencing, intelligent workload partitioning, data versioning, latest-state processing, and self-healing recovery.  Attendees will explore how partitioning transactions by business identifiers enables parallel execution while ensuring controlled processing of updates affecting shared records. Version-aware processing helps identify stale updates and prevents outdated information from overwriting newer data. Latest-state synchronization further improves resilience by retrieving authoritative business data instead of relying on potentially delayed intermediate events.  The session also examines recovery mechanisms that preserve failed transaction metadata, evaluate retry conditions, retrieve current record states, and isolate persistent failures for investigation.  Attendees will leave with practical design patterns for handling concurrency failures, strengthening data consistency, improving recovery reliability, and building distributed systems that remain predictable under challenging operating conditions.

Title: Inject a Lost Response, Then Count the Writes
Abstract: A failed response and a failed operation are different fault models. This talk starts with a local simulation in which a record is changed but the caller receives no acknowledgement. We count the resulting writes after a blind retry and after a retry under an explicitly assumed durable idempotency contract. Further cases change the payload and version precondition. The exercise shows how to state the fault window, decide what evidence is independent of the caller, and preserve an unresolved state until authoritative evidence is available. Attendees receive a small fault-scenario matrix they can adapt to their own services. This is an instructional simulation, not a chaos experiment against a deployed system.

Title: Orchestrating Under Fire: Chaos Experiments and Mesh Partition Survival with Dimensigon
Abstract: Chaos engineering traditionally tests application resilience against infrastructure failures. But what happens when the chaos hits the management and orchestration system itself? If the orchestrator cannot survive network partitioning, automated recovery mechanisms inevitably collapse.  This session shares chaos engineering experiments executed on Dimensigon mesh networks. We will inject simulated link latency, random packet loss, and split-brain network partitions to evaluate message routing resilience, `forward_or_dispatch` recovery, and distributed vault secret access. Attendees will walk away with concrete architectures for building fault-tolerant automation platforms capable of executing amidst severe network degradation.

Title: Beyond Killing Pods: Chaos Engineering for Kubernetes and Microservices
Abstract: Deleting a Kubernetes pod is easy. Understanding whether your distributed system can survive a real production failure is much harder.  Modern microservices depend on complex interactions between Kubernetes, service meshes, messaging systems, databases, and external networks. While infrastructure may recover automatically, application-level failures can still cascade through retries, timeouts, overloaded dependencies, and unexpected resource contention.  In this session, I'll explore how SRE teams can move beyond basic fault injection and design meaningful chaos experiments that test actual system resilience.  Drawing on my experience engineering and operating large-scale distributed platforms, I'll discuss how to identify critical failure scenarios, define steady-state behavior, measure blast radius, and use observability to understand how systems respond under stress.  We'll examine practical scenarios involving Kubernetes workloads, network disruptions, Kafka dependencies, and service-to-service communication, with an emphasis on making experiments safe, measurable, and actionable.  The goal is to help engineers build confidence in their recovery mechanisms before real incidents put them to the test.  Key takeaways - Design chaos experiments around realistic production failure modes. - Define measurable steady-state hypotheses and recovery criteria. - Understand cascading failures across Kubernetes, service meshes, and messaging systems. - Use observability to measure impact and validate recovery. - Turn experiment findings into concrete reliability improvements.  Intended audience SREs, platform engineers, DevOps engineers, software architects, and engineering leaders.

Title: Surviving Kubernetes Failures: HA Database Design and Chaos Testing
Abstract: Infrastructure failures are inevitable, but database outages do not have to result in prolonged service disruptions. As organizations deploy mission-critical databases on private Kubernetes clouds, maintaining availability during node failures, storage disruptions, and network outages becomes essential. Stateful workloads introduce complex challenges involving replication, failover, data consistency, and recovery.  This session explores practical strategies for designing and validating highly available database platforms on Kubernetes. Attendees will learn how synchronous and asynchronous replication, automated failover, resilient storage, and Kubernetes-native orchestration can improve database reliability during infrastructure failures.  The discussion examines StatefulSets, TiDB Operator, AlloyDB Omni Kubernetes Operator, PostgreSQL with Patroni and pg_auto_failover, MySQL Group Replication, and MariaDB Enterprise Operator. It also covers storage-class selection, resource management, network considerations, and Pod Disruption Budgets for maintaining service continuity.  A key focus is chaos engineering through controlled failure testing and gameday exercises. By simulating node failures, zonal outages, and network disruptions, teams can identify weaknesses, evaluate recovery procedures, and validate high availability strategies.  Participants will gain a practical framework for strengthening database resilience, improving recovery readiness, and maintaining reliable Kubernetes database operations.

Title: Surviving a 300% Flash Crowd: State-Safe Autoscaling With Zero Split-Brain Events
Abstract: Flash crowds expose a weak point in Kubernetes. The default autoscaler reacts only after thresholds break, and new pods take 30 to 90 seconds to become ready. During a simulated 300% surge on a stateful telemetry workload, P99 latency hit 4,200ms, and the baseline cluster recorded 14 split-brain events.  This talk walks through replacing the HPA loop with a Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) reinforcement-learning agent. Its reward function penalizes state-synchronization faults alongside SLA violations. Before any pod is killed, it runs a four-step handoff: drain, flush, reassign, terminate. The system was tested in a one-month A/B experiment across 50 bare-metal nodes, with surges from 10,000 to 40,000 RPS in under 5 seconds.  Split-brain events fell from 14 to zero, P99 latency dropped to 1.2ms, and cold starts went from 45 seconds to zero.  Attendees will learn how surge experiments expose state-safety failures, plus a scaling pattern that stays consistent under stress.

Title: Chaos Engineering Is Not Just Killing Pods: Testing Resilience in .NET Services
Abstract: Most teams try to build resilient applications by adding retries, timeouts, circuit breakers, and health checks. But an important question is often missed: have we actually tested whether those resilience mechanisms work under failure?  In this session, I will show how chaos engineering can be applied at the application level in .NET, not only at the Kubernetes or infrastructure level. Using a simple microservice-style example with an Order API calling a Payment API, we will inject controlled failures such as latency and exceptions, then observe how the system behaves when Polly-based resilience policies are triggered.  The talk will cover the difference between stability and resilience, why failures become dangerous when they spread across connected services, and how uncertainty, complexity, and emergent behavior make modern systems hard to predict. Through a practical .NET demo, we will explore retries, timeouts, circuit breakers, and fault injection using Simmy/Polly-style chaos policies.  The goal is to help developers move beyond assuming their systems are resilient and start validating resilience through safe, controlled experiments.

Title: What Happens When DNS Stops Working? Breaking Kubernetes on Purpose.
Abstract: Kubernetes makes it easy to deploy distributed applications, but what happens when one of its most fundamental dependencies becomes unreliable?  In this session, we'll deliberately introduce DNS failures into a running Kubernetes environment and explore how seemingly healthy applications start behaving unexpectedly.  Using a live demo with a small microservices application, we'll inject DNS resolution failures, examine their impact on service-to-service communication, and investigate how retry policies, connection pooling, DNS caching, and readiness probes influence application behavior.  We'll then experiment with different recovery strategies and compare their effectiveness under failure.

Title: When the Fixer Breaks: Failure-Mode Thinking for Autonomous IT Operations Agents
Abstract: Agentic AI promises to shift IT operations from reactive ticket handling to predicting and fixing problems before users notice. But an agent that can remediate an endpoint can also remediate the wrong one. Resilience has to cover the automation itself, not only the systems it manages.  This talk uses the Autonomous Digital Operations Framework (ADOF), a conceptual six-layer architecture, as a case for failure-mode thinking. ADOF combines endpoint telemetry, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), and six specialized agents, including Incident Prediction, Asset Health, and Procurement Intelligence. The talk covers:  Failure scenarios worth testing: stale or missing telemetry, outdated knowledge returned by retrieval, and incorrect predictions How composite scores (Enterprise Health, Business Impact, and Automation Confidence) serve as a safety boundary, with agents acting above 85% confidence and escalating below 60% Why confidence should drop, not hold steady, when input data degrades How a five-level maturity model limits the impact radius of agent errors while autonomy grows  ADOF is proposed for future validation. Viewers will leave with a practical checklist of failure modes to test before giving AI agents operational authority.

Title: Engineering Self-Healing Retail Systems with Agentic AI and Failure Recovery
Abstract: Distributed retail platforms depend on interconnected services for ordering, payments, inventory, loyalty programs, and delivery. When failures occur, traditional monitoring often generates alerts without coordinating remediation or validating recovery. This session explores how Agentic AI can strengthen operational resilience through intelligent failure detection, policy-driven remediation, and controlled service restoration.  The session presents a proposed Autonomous Retail Operations Agent built around five stages: detecting abnormal service behavior, recommending corrective actions, executing policy-approved temporary store disablement, enabling human-initiated recovery, and validating system health before reopening.  Using a representative scenario involving sustained transaction failures, attendees will explore how event streaming, AI-assisted diagnosis, deterministic policy checks, and automated notifications can coordinate incident response. The architecture addresses challenges such as distinguishing isolated errors from persistent failures, reducing alert fatigue, preventing transactions during disruptions, and avoiding premature recovery.  The discussion also examines how health validation, role-based permissions, and auditable recovery policies support safer automation in distributed environments. Attendees will gain practical architectural insights into designing bounded AI agents for resilient retail operations, with future considerations including predictive failure detection, cross-store correlation, and digital twins.

Title: Solving the Run Phase: The Next Bottleneck for AI Agents
Abstract: We figured out how to build agents. Anyone can stand up an impressive single-team demo. The run is where it stalls: data that isn't ready, trust and governance left unresolved, integration that costs more than planned, and pilots that never become a live service.  Deployed is not the same as live. Live needs a named business owner, an accountable service owner, access and action boundaries, a support and rollback path, and a way to reassess when models, tools or context change. Those decisions can be named in advance, and that is where the bottleneck now sits: with us, People & Processes.  This session maps the run phase as an operating model. Choose the route first: adopt SaaS, combine it with shared context and controls, or build and resource a platform. Form and name the team that builds and the team that runs. Then run a shared agent platform with a named owner (identity, tool connections, runtime controls, evaluation, telemetry and cost, governed context) so the next squad inherits rather than rebuilds, with a Centre of Excellence feeding improvements back.  For reliability teams, the focus is on agreeing access and action boundaries, support and rollback before live use, and deciding when a change to a model, tool or context requires fresh evaluation. You'll leave with a practical checklist for the team that owns the run.

Title: We let AI agents touch production. Here is what the platform had to give them
Abstract: José Escrich's team spent two years building agents that investigate and fix production incidents, then ran them on real on-call rotations at three companies. Most of what broke was not the model; it was the platform. This is the field report.  Key takeaways: - The four primitives an agent needs before it can act safely: read-only telemetry, a registry of signed actions, an approval gate that fits in a page, and a place to write back what it learned. - Why "human in the loop" as the only step kills adoption, and how approval as the last step changed engineer behaviour. - What the Opsgenie sunset forces platform teams to decide in 2027, and how to redesign on-call instead of just migrating it. - The failure modes nobody warned about: privilege creep, cost blow-ups, confidently wrong agents.

Title: How Azure SRE Agent supports your Chaos Engineering streams
Abstract: We had Agile, Scrum and DevOps to optimize how to run our datacenters both on-premises and in public cloud. Are you ready for the next step, where it is not just about deploying and migrating workloads to cloud, but also running them in an efficient and healthy way. To do that, you need to have reliable tools and provide observability capabilities to your teams. Good news is that Azure offers all of that, and more. Learn in this session from Peter De Tender - Senior Content Developer for DevOps Solutions - about the fundamentals of Site Resiliency Engineering, and how Azure SRE Agent should be part of your toolbelt as Chaos Engineer.

Title: Replay-Safe Architecture: Failure Testing Event-Driven Recovery
Abstract: Kafka is healthy. Consumer lag is zero. Dashboards are green. Then someone finds a bounded gap in downstream business state.  This talk is about the uncomfortable part of chaos engineering for event-driven recovery: proving that recovery repaired the business state instead of just replaying records successfully.  We will walk through a production-shaped incident in an inventory platform where a damaged interval of events forces a series of architectural questions: which range is safe to replay, which identity protects the business effect, where idempotency actually lives, how long dedupe evidence must survive, what happens when historical events meet current policy, and how to keep repair traffic from becoming the next incident.  The core claim is simple: availability tells us the machinery is running; replayability tells us whether we can reconstruct, repair, and trust state after damage. Attendees will leave with a practical recovery checklist for event-driven systems: separate delivery guarantees from business-effect guarantees, name the idempotency and ordering boundaries, preserve enough evidence for audit, bound blast radius with approval and rate controls, and close incidents with reconciliation proof rather than job completion.

Title: Your Backup Is Not Your Recovery: Rebuilding API Trust Without Rebuilding the Breach
Abstract: Most resilience planning asks one question after an incident: how fast can we get back up? After a cyber incident, that question is dangerous. The fastest restore often reinstates the long-lived credentials, broad service permissions, network-based trust, and undocumented dependencies that made the system fragile in the first place. NIST SP 800-207, SP 800-207A, and SP 800-184 define zero trust and recovery, but leave the transition between them undefined.  This talk presents a five-step method for using the recovery window to reduce fragility rather than restore it. Teams map API dependencies across seven attributes, including privilege, business criticality, and exposure to compromised infrastructure, then contain compromised credentials, introduce an identity-centered API control plane, apply risk-adaptive authorization, and modernize progressively from the highest-risk interfaces.  Instead of a binary allow or deny, which turns every policy decision into a potential outage, authorization supports six graded outcomes: allow, restricted, read-only, step-up authentication, quarantine, and deny. This lets systems degrade gracefully under suspicion instead of failing hard. An enforcement gateway wraps legacy APIs without rewrites, and seven indicators, such as implicit trust paths removed and mean time to revoke access, track progress on a synthetic API dependency graph.  Attendees will leave with a recovery approach that treats every incident as a chance to remove hidden failure paths.

Title: The Probabilities Have Flipped: Chaos Engineering for Metro-Wide and Regional Data Center Loss
Abstract: n 2026, simultaneous multi-availability zone and data center outages shifted from hypothetical risk models to hard operational reality—taking out major cloud infrastructure across the UAE and Russia, with some fintech services requiring up to 11 days to recover. Traditional disaster recovery assumes that losing a physical facility is an edge case and that multiple availability zones provide sufficient isolation. They don't: availability zones within a single metro area share correlated physical and grid failure domains.  Moving disaster recovery from static runbooks to active Chaos Engineering, this session breaks down how to empirically test and survive regional blast radiuses:  Challenging Core DR Hypotheses: Why multiple AZs are not a DR strategy, why "zero RPO" does not exist under catastrophic partitions, and how to determine acceptable data loss upfront.  Decoupling Control and Data Planes: Architecting backup orchestration, state machines, and failover control planes strictly outside the primary blast radius.  Testing Reserve Capacity: Validating dynamic failover agreements and cross-region provisioning under simulated stress rather than paying for idle multi-region parity.  Autonomous Pre-emptive Failover: Exploring AI agents that monitor external telemetry (grid signals, physical threat vectors, critical zero-days) to trigger chaos-tested failover sequences before the cloud provider acknowledges the outage.  Attendees will walk away with concrete patterns for structuring regional GameDays and transforming recovery assumptions into validated, production-ready chaos experiments.

Title: Break Your Own Agent: A Blast-Radius Experiment on 'Isolated' AI Subagents
Abstract: Agent frameworks call their subagents "isolated". That can mean a separate conversation, or it can mean a security boundary. This talk tests which one you get, as a chaos experiment. In each run, we look at the blast radius: what the subagent can reach.  The hypothesis is that a read-only subagent cannot leak secrets, because it has no write tool and no edit tool. To test it, we clone a repo. Its README asks for a routine environment check. The script behind that check prints every variable with "key", "secret" or "token" in its name.  Experiment 1 runs on the host. The hypothesis fails. The tool limit holds, because a blocked tool has no handler in the code. But the child process inherits the full environment of the parent. The keys move from the subagent output to the parent context and then to the session log.  Experiment 2 runs the same task in plain Docker, with one key passed in with "-e". Only that key leaks. The other secrets are out of reach.  Experiment 3 uses Docker Sandboxes. The sandbox gets a placeholder token, and a proxy swaps in the real token on egress. The process inside never sees the real credential.  We use decoy credentials and one open-source agent, "pi", pinned to one version. Its docs say it has no built-in sandbox, which makes it a fair test subject.  The talk ends with three questions to ask about any "isolated" agent: - The talk ends with three questions to ask about any "isolated" agent: - Does the child scope its credentials or inherit them? - Is the boundary an OS, a VM, a container, or a proxy, or only a separate conversation?  We also map the tool limit to the OWASP Agentic AI Top 10. It partly covers ASI02 (tool misuse) and does nothing for ASI03 (identity and privilege abuse).

Title: Chaos Engineering for Policy: Injecting Poisoned Rules Into AI-Agent Guardrails
Abstract: Chaos engineering injects faults into infrastructure to see what breaks. This talk applies the same idea one layer up, to the *policy* that guards AI coding agents. Guardrail rules are increasingly mined from postmortems, runbooks, tickets and chat; what happens when some of them are wrong, tampered with, or forged?  I built a fault-injection benchmark to find out: **500 Kubernetes and Terraform constraints** seeded from public postmortems and the OPA Gatekeeper library, with 18 kinds of poisoning injected (tampered provenance hashes, forged principals, rules asserted by people with no authority, stale copies, injected text), and a steady-state hypothesis expressed as a metric, **poison susceptibility**: how much poisoned policy does the guardrail act on, without over-blocking the legitimate changes? - OPA/Rego and deny-list hooks acted on **100%** of injected faults. - An LLM self-check with the organisation's authority map still acted on **52%**. - Provenance plus authority checks got to **zero**.  You will leave with a repeatable way to run policy-poisoning experiments against your own hooks and admission controllers, the blast-radius patterns we saw, and the open-source corpus and harness to do it.

Title: Securing Agentforce MCP Integrations Against Seven CRM Failure Risks
Abstract: Enterprise AI agents introduce security and reliability risks when untrusted CRM data influences automated decisions and tool execution. In Salesforce Agentforce deployments, customer-submitted case descriptions, knowledge articles, and account histories can become attack surfaces that protocol-level MCP defenses alone cannot adequately protect.  This session examines seven CRM-native integration risks: case description injection, knowledge base poisoning, account history manipulation, SOQL injection through MCP query parameters, tool result manipulation, data exfiltration through webhooks, and permission escalation through tool chaining.  Attendees will explore how these risks can compromise agent behavior and how Salesforce-native controls help reduce exposure. Practical mitigation approaches include Agent Script deterministic gates, Apex wrappers with parameterized SOQL and allowlists, Connected App outbound restrictions, tool-chain depth limits, and Shield monitoring.  The session organizes these safeguards into four engineering layers: input validation, reasoning isolation, execution governance, and output monitoring. Through concrete CRM integration scenarios, attendees will learn how to identify potential failure paths, strengthen execution controls, and improve the security and reliability of Agentforce deployments.

Title: We attacked our own AI agent memory: 30 adversarial writes, one hole, one fix
Abstract: FleetMemory is an open-source shared memory for a fleet of AI agents. An agent can propose a fact, but the fact only becomes memory if it traces to something a customer actually said. Claims without a source go to quarantine, and an LLM verifier that defaults to reject rules on them. If the verifier call fails, that counts as a rejection too.  Then we tried to break it. We ran 30 adversarial writes across 5 attack classes against the real gate and verifier, not a mock. The first run found a hole: a brand-new fact that contradicted nothing already in memory walked straight in, 6 times out of 6. The fix was one rule, needs_provenance, and after it the same 30 attacks were all blocked.  The gate still isn't perfect, and the talk shows where. It let through 9 of 10 legitimate customer updates. The one it missed is a race condition we left visible in the decision journal instead of tuning it away. Median gate latency over the run was 293 ms. The red-team script and results are in the public repo, so you can rerun them against your own agent memory.

Title: Sandboxing an AI Agent Is Not One Decision, It's Four
Abstract: Every framework that lets an AI agent write and run its own code eventually asks the same question: how much of that code should execute inside a sandbox, and how much stays outside as trusted orchestration. The common answer treats sandboxing as one API with one security level, pick a container image and move on. Real systems need at least four distinct boundaries, and they are not a ladder from less secure to more secure, each one isolates a different unit of work for a different reason. Restricted code orchestration keeps a credentialed agent in charge and lets it call only pre-registered tools, nothing new ever actually executes. Sandboxed code execution as a tool crosses a real line: model-generated code runs somewhere the credentialed agent cannot reach, called like any other tool. Sandboxed command execution moves an entire author-defined job into isolation, with its own lifecycle for files, artifacts, cancellation, and reconnection after a dropped connection. Sandboxed task execution goes further still, moving a worker's complete instruction set into a remote executor that owns the whole task lifecycle end to end. Picking the wrong boundary either leaves a real code-execution hole open or pays isolation costs a workload never needed. I will walk through this taxonomy using real, ongoing work inside Apache Airflow's agentic execution model, show a live example at each of the four positions, and give the audience a concrete way to reason about their own agent architecture instead of reaching for "just run it in a container."

Title: Trust me, bro? Is not a security stratergy in an agentic ai framework.
Abstract: Every product team is being asked to add "our own AI". The demo takes a day; the trouble starts after that. I follow Skhumba, a fictional delivery company's AI assistant, from demo to production across eight layers of a real AI stack: model, system prompt, retrieval, tools (MCP), access control, guardrails, cost control and observability. Each fix creates the next problem. It recommends a competitor. It invents a refund limit because it never saw the policy. Once it has tools, it reads payroll data to a new hire and obeys a hidden instruction in a customer email. Then 2,000 people ask at once and the token bill explodes. Even a Friday prompt change that skips the evals brings the first bug back. At every failure the audience decides what to do, then we see the fix and what it costs. The scenarios are illustrative, built to show patterns developers will meet, not measurements from one production system. As AI agents join everyday business workflows, trust alone is not enough, and "trust me, bro" is not a security strategy. This session turns AI governance, security and responsible adoption into concrete engineering decisions a team can make on Monday.  What attendees take away 1.Who the agent acts as and what it may touch: narrow tool permissions and human approval for consequential actions reduce the damage when an injection gets through. Filters and detection alone do not make injection safe. 2.How to test prompt and model changes before they ship, and why the change that skips the evals is the one that brings old bugs back. 3.How to trace failures across model, retrieval, tools and cost - investigating inputs, tool calls and failures - and who owns the system when it acts badly.

Title: Chaos at the Edge Case: Interaction-Only Failures in Safety-Critical Autonomous Systems
Abstract: Most fault-injection campaigns test one failure at a time: kill a sensor, degrade an actuator, see what breaks. But in safety-critical autonomous systems, the scariest failures often live at the edge case where two individually "safe" degradations overlap — and single-fault chaos testing walks right past them.  We ran this experiment on an autonomous emergency braking (AEB) system. A sensing delay, tested alone, was fine. A reduced braking capability, tested alone, was fine. Combined, across 5,544 simulated scenarios, 209 cases turned out hazardous only in combination — invisible to either single-fault test. A follow-up fault-injection pass added realistic brake-actuator lag and re-tested every one of those 209 edge cases: more than half survived the harder model, and the reason the rest didn't is the most useful part of the story.  This talk covers how we defined, located, and prioritized these "interaction-only" failures: a deterministic parameter sweep, a 200,000-run Monte Carlo campaign, and a margin-based boundary analysis simple enough to run against your own failure-mode matrix. We'll also cover the concrete next step — targeted high-fidelity simulation of the worst boundary cases — for teams who need to close the gap between "found in chaos testing" and "validated for production."

Title: The value that is eventually right: a tenth-of-a-second window on iOS, and why every test that waits cannot see it
Abstract: Ask a phone for a portrait video in the browser and the file comes back sideways. I spent three nights assuming it was my code. Then I built a test page and it said there was no bug, four times in a row. The one fact that would not fit: the same phone, in the same ten minutes, still recorded sideways when the fix was off.  The cause is a window. For the first 112 to 139 milliseconds the camera track reports the sensor's landscape size, then corrects itself at the first painted frame. Read inside the window and you get the wrong shape. Read after it and everything is fine. Every one of my clean tests waited for the preview before reading, which put it on the safe side of the window every time. A test written without knowing the window exists cannot see the bug, no matter how carefully it is written.  That is a resilience story, not a camera story. Any value that is eventually right will pass a test that waits for things to settle, and fail in production for the code that did not wait. A fixed delay is not a fix, it is a race you will eventually lose that also taxes every user who did not need it. The signal you want is the event that makes the value true, not the clock.  This talk is the measurement, taken on a real iPhone with timing tables, what the failure looked like inside a production SDK that had carried the bug for thirteen months with three reporters, and what happened when the window was written down: Apple's WebKit team triaged the report as a regression the next day, and LiveKit shipped one fix in six hours and a second four days later from a gap I found reviewing the first.  What the talk covers, pre-recorded, about 30 minutes:  1. The symptom, two clips from the same phone, fix off and fix on. 2. Four clean test runs and the fact that would not fit. How a test settles onto the wrong side of a window. 3. The measurement. Read the value the moment it exists and keep reading. 1920 by 1080 at once, 1080 by 1920 at the first frame, 112 ms and 139 ms across two runs. Why the number moves with device, camera, resolution and load. 4. The production failure. A year-old issue in a widely used video SDK: a 10 ms sleep, then poll until the value exists. It exists immediately and it is wrong, so a portrait phone announces itself as landscape to everyone on the call. 5. Why a longer sleep is not the fix. Two runs, two numbers. Any constant is a race. 6. Two fixes with code: wait for the event that makes the value true, or measure the truth directly and never trust the report. 7. How to write the test that would have caught it, and the general rule: name the event that makes your value true, and gate on that, never on time. 8. What happened when the window was written down. Report to first fix in six hours, second fix in four days.  Takeaways: an eventually-correct value passes every test that waits. Gate on the event, not the clock. When a report and the real thing disagree, the real thing is the evidence. Measure the window before you argue about the delay.

Title: Behavioral Regression Testing for LLM Systems: Chaos Engineering for a Dependency You Do Not Control
Abstract: Chaos engineering assumes you can inject the fault. With a hosted model you cannot. The provider upgrades the model on their schedule, behavior shifts underneath you with no deploy on your side, and the first signal is often a support ticket rather than an alert. The dependency is nondeterministic, it is versioned by someone else, and it fails by being subtly wrong instead of by returning an error.  This talk covers how to build a deliberate practice around that. We start with eval-as-code: a behavioral suite that runs in CI on every prompt change, every retrieval change, and every model swap, with pass thresholds that gate the deploy rather than emailing a report nobody reads. We cover how to pick cases that actually catch regressions, including the adversarial and edge inputs that only show up once you have production traffic to mine.  Then we move to the faults you can inject. Degrade the model tier and see whether quality holds. Return empty or contradictory retrieval and see whether the system says it does not know or invents an answer. Truncate context and watch which instruction gets dropped. Introduce latency on a tool and see whether the orchestration degrades gracefully or stalls. Replay traffic against a candidate model before the provider forces the move.  We finish on drift detection in production: sampling live outputs into the same eval harness, tracking scores as a time series rather than a one-time gate, and alerting on the shape of the distribution rather than on individual failures.  Takeaways: A CI-enforced behavioral regression suite. A catalog of injectable faults for LLM and retrieval systems. Drift detection that catches a silent provider-side change before users do.  Audience: SREs, ML and AI engineers, platform teams. Level: Intermediate to advanced.

Title: The Queue Is Empty, but Something Is Wrong: Chaos Testing Beyond Health Checks
Abstract: Imagine a ticketing system where a worker crashes after saving a seat assignment, but before marking the job as complete. The job gets retried, the worker finishes successfully, and the queue is empty. Everything looks fine. But the event now has more confirmed seats than it can hold.  How can a system look healthy after recovery while still producing the wrong result?  In this talk, I’ll walk through a small experiment I built using Go and PostgreSQL. It models a paid waitlist where each person should either get a confirmed seat or receive a refund. I’ll show how worker crashes, retries, and races can lead to problems that a final health check does not catch.  We’ll compare two versions of the workers: one with deliberate implementation mistakes and another that handles the scenarios safely. I’ll demonstrate how to inject faults at specific points, control the order in which workers run, and check the final result against business rules.  The takeaway is simple: a worker can recover and the queue can be empty while the result is still wrong. To catch that, we need to check what happened to users—not just whether the workers finished.  The project uses synthetic data and deliberately introduced bugs. It is a reproducible case study, not a test of a real ticketing platform.

Title: Designing for Failure: Practical Chaos Engineering in Cloud Systems
Abstract: Modern cloud systems are distributed, complex, and inherently failure-prone. Yet most engineering teams still design for ideal conditions rather than real-world failure scenarios.  This talk explores chaos engineering as a practical discipline for improving system resilience in cloud-native architectures. Using real-world cloud architecture examples, we examine how controlled failure injection exposes hidden weaknesses before they impact production users.  We will cover:  What chaos engineering is (beyond theory) How to safely introduce failure in cloud environments (AWS/Kubernetes patterns) The role of observability in detecting and diagnosing system degradation Common architectural failure modes in distributed systems How to start implementing chaos experiments incrementally in real production systems  By the end, attendees will understand how to move from reactive incident response to proactive resilience engineering using structured chaos experiments grounded in real system design.

Title: Predicting the Blast Radius, Then Spending Your One Experiment
Abstract: Chaos engineering asks an honest question: what breaks? Then it answers it by breaking it. That works, and it's why most teams don't do it. The experiment costs money, it costs pager load, and in production it costs customers, so the team that would learn the most is the team that runs it least.  This talk argues for a cheaper first move. Predict the blast radius of a change before you make it, then spend your one experiment on whatever the prediction couldn't settle.  I'll show it on a real infrastructure change rather than a diagram: what a modelled run says about p99, error rate and cost before anything is applied, and what it deliberately refuses to say. Then the harder half, which is knowing when a prediction is lying to you. A report that infers a pass from incomplete evidence is worse than no report, and a prediction that can't tell you which of its conclusions are estimated is theatre.  The useful position is neither. Predict what you can, mark what you can't, and let the experiment pay for itself by answering the one question the model couldn't.
